subject: Brightleaf performance discovery — options & next steps
messages:
From: Jonas Weber <jonas.weber@redwood.com>

Subject: Brightleaf performance discovery — options & next steps

Hi Alex / Priya,

Thanks again for the time this morning — helpful to see the product flow. I promised a short recap so the team has a single source of truth before we follow up with a draft SLO and a quick benchmark run. Below is what I captured, plus a proposed set of next steps. Please correct anything I missed.

Summary of requirements (from call)
- Workload: personalization & in-session suggestions (multi-turn).
- Latency target: p95 target between 150ms and 250ms for single-turn suggestion responses (streaming acceptable for longer outputs).
- Baseline throughput: ~80 requests/sec sustained for the core region (US-EAST).
- Burst behavior: spikes up to ~400 req/sec during promotional events, with ~10–15s burst durations expected.
- Concurrency: typical concurrent users ~40, occasional peaks to ~250 when multiple sessions require KV lookups.
- Streaming: progressive suggestion delivery is desired for a snappy UX (partial tokens streamed).
- Availability: prefer a Dedicated or Private deployment for data separation; happy to start with Hosted for discovery.

Primary constraints / priorities you mentioned
- Latency > cost; but they still want clear unit economics to evaluate a pilot.
- Determinism: consistent p95 is more important than absolute best-case p50.
- Predictable autoscale for promo events is a must.

Proposed follow-ups (short timeline)
1) Redwood: share a short SLO draft and 2 candidate config profiles (low-latency, cost-optimized) — by EOD Monday. (Marissa will attach initial bench numbers.)
2) Brightleaf: confirm which flows need streaming vs single-shot responses so we can prioritize prefixes to cache — by early next week.
3) Joint: schedule a 60-minute bench session to validate p95 at a representative workload (we can run 1–2 quick runs in our staging pool) — proposed times in the doc we’ll share.

I’m attaching a brief placeholder SLO and the slots we have for a run next week.

Regards,
Jonas
Director, Solutions — Redwood Inference

Attachments: BRF-slo-draft.pdf (short SLO + checklist), benchmarks-nov2026.csv (sample microbenchmarks)

Thanks Jonas — that's a great summary and matches our internal notes. Couple of quick clarifications:  

- The 150–250ms p95 is for the MOST frequent suggestion path (single-item suggestion). For multi-item batched suggestions we can accept higher p95 (up to 400ms) as long as initial token streaming starts <120ms.
- Streaming: We want token-by-token streaming for the first partial suggestion only; rest can batch.
- Caching: we expect a ~25% repeat prefix rate on the personalization queries during normal traffic, higher during promos.

Two asks from our side before the bench:  
1) Can you outline the expected cost delta between a 4-bit quantized model and an 8-bit profile for our workload? Ballpark is fine.
2) When you talk about autoscale for bursts, can you do a quick note on cold-start behavior (how long to spin up extra pods and whether warm standby helps)?

If you can include that in the SLO doc, we can sign off on the bench slots. Also available Fri 11/29 10–11am ET for a quick sync.

—Alex
Senior Engineering Manager | Brightleaf Retail
From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
To: Alex Hunter <alex.hunter@brightleafretail.com>, Priya Shah <priya.shah@brightleafretail.com>
Cc: Jonas Weber <jonas.weber@redwood.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-11-28T13:45:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Brightleaf performance discovery — options & next steps

Alex / Priya — thanks, this is actionable. I pulled a few concise notes and a recommended starter configuration. See below and the attached benchmark CSV for microbench numbers from our staging run with a proxy dataset similar to yours.

Quick answer to your asks
- Cost delta (ballpark): 4-bit quantized model (int4/qlora-ish runtime) can reduce GPU memory footprint by ~2.5–3x vs fp16 and lower per-token GPU cost by ~30–45% depending on kernel efficiency. 8-bit (int8) sits between: ~1.6–2x memory reduction vs fp16 and ~15–25% token-cost reduction. Real numbers depend heavily on seq length distribution and attention kernels for the chosen model family.
- Autoscale + cold start: for our Dedicated pools with a warm hot-standby policy, spin-up to additional instances to handle a burst (400 req/s) typically takes ~60–90s if a new VM/GPU is needed; warm standby (pre-warmed instances kept at low cost) can reduce that to ~5–15s. We recommend a hybrid policy for promo events: maintain a small warm buffer and allow extra burst capacity.

Recommended starter configs (two profiles)
1) Low-latency profile (prioritize p95):
   - Dedicated pool, c5-large-like (gpu-optimized) instances with 1.2x baseline capacity.
   - Model variant: int8 quantized variant of chosen family (better latency determinism than int4 in our runs).
   - Continuous batching: small batch windows (5–15ms) with adaptive early-flush for tails.
   - KV/prefix caching: aggressive prefix cache for top 25% of prefixes (saves ~40–55ms p95 in our bench).
   - Streaming: enable progressive token flush after first token generated.
   - Expected p95 from our staging run: ~160–240ms at 80 req/s sustained (see attached).

2) Cost-optimized profile (balance cost + acceptable latency):
   - Hosted/Dedicated mixed routing (route regular to hosted cheaper pool; long-tail to dedicated).
   - Model variant: int4 quantized (aggressive) for non-critical paths; int8 for critical suggestion path.
   - Continuous batching: slightly larger windows (20–40ms) to increase throughput efficiency.
   - Cache: selective caching for high-repeat keys only.
   - Expected p95: 220–380ms for mixed workloads; cost estimate: ~30–45% lower unit GPU cost vs low-latency profile.

Tradeoffs and notes
- Int4 gives best cost but more variable latencies (we observed occasional +80–120ms spikes on tails in microbench). If determinism matters, int8 is a safer starting point.
- Continuous batching reduces token cost, but increases p95 tail unless early flush heuristics are tuned per traffic distribution.
- Prefix/KV caching has huge win for repeated conversational contexts — if your repeat-rate is >20% we see >30% p95 improvement without extra compute.

Attachments: benchmarks-nov2026.csv contains run configs and p95/p50 rows for typical seq lengths (32/64/128) and batch window tests. I've also dropped a short SLO draft in BRF-slo-draft.pdf that maps requirements to observability checkpoints.

Short next steps proposal
- We provision a 2-hour bench run in our staging Dedicated pool (int8 profile) to validate p95 at 80 req/s and a 2-minute burst at 400 req/s.
- If the bench meets targets, we'll run a short pilot for 48 hours on a mixed-hosted route to surface production variability.

I can join the Fri 11/29 10–11am ET slot to walk through the bench plan and the SLO. If that works, I’ll send a calendar invite.

Best,
Marissa Cole
Solutions Engineer — Redwood Inference
